Likewise the sorrow of Rama too is to be known, O Pandava, hearing which men and women fall into greater bewilderment.
shivpurana:7:38.21	So I cannot describe it again. Regard the body as a heap of sorrow; it is to be given up now.
shivpurana:7:38.22	Whoever has taken it on is pervaded by it, without doubt. First, birth in the mother's womb is a cause of sorrow;
shivpurana:7:38.23	in childhood too there is great sorrow in following childish play; then in youth, enjoying pleasures that are sorrow in form,
shivpurana:7:38.24	with the coming and going of days and many burdens of work, life wastes away daily and one does not know it.
shivpurana:7:38.25	At the end comes death, the greatest sorrow of all, and then ignorant men suffer the torments of many hells.
shivpurana:7:38.26	So this is unreal; you should practise the real. A man should do whatever pleases Shambhu.
Nandishvara said: Thus with various talk the brothers all passed their time again on the paths of their hopes.
Arjuna too, going himself among the difficult mountains, firm in his vow, having found a Yaksha and slaying many robbers with him,
joyful in mind, went to the excellent mountain; going there, to a lovely spot near the Ganga,
[they said to Arjuna:] "This task is to be accomplished by you and never by another; by Vyasa's word it is clear — make your life fruitful."
where there is an ashoka grove like excellent heaven, he stayed there, having bathed and bowed to his excellent teacher.
He himself adopted the dress and the rest as instructed, and first withdrawing his senses, he became established in mind.
Again, making a beautiful, well-proportioned earthen image, he meditated before it on the unsurpassed mass of radiance.
Bathing well three times a day, he performed various worship there and served Hara again and again.
Seeing the radiance issuing from his head, Indra's spies were afraid: "When did this one enter?"
Reflecting again, "This must be told to Vidaujas (Indra)," they went quickly to Shakra.
The spies said: "O lord of gods, a god or a sage, the Sun or Fire, is performing austerity in the forest; we do not know who he is.
Burnt by his radiance, we have come to you; his conduct has been reported — let what is fitting be done."
Nandishvara said: Told this by the spies, knowing everything his son intended, he dismissed the guardians of the mountains and resolved to go there.
Becoming an old brahmin, a celibate student, the husband of Shachi went there, O best of brahmins, to test him.
Having said this to Arjuna, they, distressed by longing at the separation, sent him there respectfully though unwilling.
Seeing him arrive, the Pandava worshipped him, stood before him, praised him and said, "Tell me now, where have you come from?"
Addressed thus, the lord of gods, to test his steadfastness, lovingly spoke to the Pandava words that concealed a test:
The brahmin said: "In your fresh youth, dear one, why are you doing austerity now? Is all this austerity of yours for liberation or for victory?"
Nandishvara said: Asked thus, he told everything again; hearing it, the brahmin spoke again:
The brahmin said: "It is not fitting, hero, to perform austerity to gain happiness; it should be done with the kshatriya's dharma, for liberation, best of the Kurus.

Indra is the giver of happiness, but he cannot be the giver of liberation; so, best one, you should perform true austerity in every way." Nandishvara said: Hearing these words, Arjuna grew angry; humble-minded and of good vows, disregarding them, he replied:
Arjuna said: "Not for a kingdom and not for liberation — why do you say this? Such austerity is done at Vyasa's word.
Go from here, celibate; you wish to make me fall. What business do you, a celibate student, have here?"
Nandishvara said: Addressed thus, he was pleased and showed his own wondrous, beautiful form with its accoutrements.
Draupadi, full of sorrow, holding back the tears in her eyes, the faithful wife, spoke auspicious words as she sent him off:
Seeing Shakra's form, Arjuna was ashamed; Indra reassured him and spoke again:
Indra said: "Choose a boon, dear Dhananjaya, great-minded one; whatever your heart desires, there is nothing I will not give you."
Hearing Shakra's words, Arjuna replied, "Give me victory, dear one, oppressed as I am by enemies in every way."
Shakra said: "Your enemies led by Duryodhana are very strong — Drona, Bhishma and Karna are all surely hard to conquer;
Ashvatthama, Drona's son, a portion of Rudra, is exceedingly invincible. They would be impossible for me in every way; hear what is for your good.
No one can now bring about this victory, hero; Shiva is the best, so now recite Shambhu's mantra.
Shankara, lord of all worlds, lord of the moving and unmoving, self-ruling, is able to do everything and grants the fruit of enjoyment and liberation.
I, Brahma and the others, and Vishnu, giver of all boons, and all others who seek victory — all are worshippers of Shiva.
From today, leaving that mantra, worship Shiva with devotion, by the procedure of the earthen image and by meditation on Shiva,
with many offerings and with your whole being, O Bharata; success will be unshakable for you today; there is no doubt."
Draupadi said: "O king, what Vyasa has taught must be done by you with effort; may your path be auspicious, and may Shankara bring you good."
Nandishvara said: Having said this, he called all the spies and told them, "Always stand watchful in protecting him."
Having instructed his spies in Arjuna's protection and the like, Indra, his heart full of affection, spoke again to the monkey-bannered one:
Indra said: "You must never neglect your kingdom out of heedlessness; may this knowledge be for your good, dear one, scorcher of foes.
The practitioner should always keep steadfastness; Shiva is the protector, and he will give you prosperity and fruit; there is no doubt."
Nandishvara said: Having given this boon to the Bharata, the lord of gods, remembering Shiva's lotus feet, went to his own abode.
Arjuna too, the great hero, bowing low to the lord of gods, performed austerity with self-control, directed to Shiva as prescribed.
All of them stayed there, having respectfully sent Arjuna away, the five together, fallen into great sorrow.
Staying there, they said, "Listen, best of sages: even in sorrow the company of loved ones does not bring sorrow;
in separation sorrow is always doubled; how can even the steadfast keep steadfastness here?"
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, third book, the Shatarudra Samhita, chapter 39: in the description of the Kirata incarnation, the slaying of the demon Muka. Nandishvara said: Having bathed duly and performed the placements and the rest duly, he performed with true devotion the meditation on Shiva as Vyasa had taught.
Meanwhile a demon named Muka came, taking the form of a boar, sent by the evil-souled
Duryodhana, the deceiver, against Arjuna, O best of brahmins, by the path where Arjuna was staying,
shattering the mountain's peaks and many trees, making various noises and moving with great speed.
Arjuna, seeing that asura named Muka, remembered Shiva's lotus feet and became intent on reflection.
Arjuna said: "Who is this, and where does he come from? He looks cruel in his deeds; he is surely coming to harm me, without doubt.
So my mind tells me: he is surely an enemy. Many Daityas and Danavas were slain by me before;
one of theirs is coming to take revenge, or some friend working for Duryodhana's good.
One on seeing whom one's mind is pleased is surely a well-wisher; one on seeing whom it is disturbed is surely an enemy.
Conduct declares the family, the body declares the food, speech declares learning, the eye declares affection.
By shape, gait, gesture and speech, by changes in the eyes and face, the hidden mind is known.
Standing on the sole of one foot like the best of sages, with his gaze fixed on the sun, he remained repeating the mantra.
The wise declare the eye to be of four kinds, with distinct meanings: bright, tender, crooked and reddened —
bright on meeting a friend, tender on seeing a son, crooked in union with a woman, and reddened on seeing an enemy.
At this one all my senses are troubled; he must be an enemy, to be killed without doubt.
And my teacher's word is present to me today: 'One who gives you sorrow must be killed in every way, O king'; there is no need to consider.
For this purpose are my weapons, without doubt." Reflecting thus, he stood right there, fitting an arrow.
Meanwhile, to protect Arjuna and to test his devotion, Shankara, kind to devotees,
quickly taking the most wondrous form of a clever Bhilla, with his hosts, came to destroy that demon,
Hara with his garment girded with creepers, his hair bound, white lines on his body, himself with bow and arrows,
bearing a quiver of arrows on his back, he went; and his host became likewise, and Shiva became king of the Bhillas.
Making various cries, the leader of the host set out and followed the boar, and the sound filled the ten directions.
He performed austerity with great love, remembering Shiva in his mind, reciting Shambhu's five-syllable mantra, the best of the best.
Arjuna was disturbed by the sound of the forest-dweller, and the mountains and all else were disturbed by those sounds.

Ah, can this be Shiva, the bringer of good here? I have heard it before, and Krishna told it again,
shivpurana:7:39.32	and Vyasa told it, and the gods remember it: Shiva is declared the bringer of good and the bringer of happiness,
shivpurana:7:39.33	and he himself is declared the giver of liberation, without doubt; by remembering his name good surely comes to men.
shivpurana:7:39.34	For those who worship him with their whole being there is no sorrow even in dreams; if ever it arises, it is born of karma,
shivpurana:7:39.35	and even if it seems much, it is surely little; or it is especially to be known as the fault of prarabdha;
shivpurana:7:39.36	or Shankara, having made one pass through what must be enjoyed, much or little, sometimes removes it by his will, without doubt.
shivpurana:7:39.37	He can make poison nectar or nectar poison; whatever he wishes he does; being able, what can be forbidden him?
shivpurana:7:39.38	Thus reflected ancient devotees and others, and so do future devotees always, bringing the mind here to steadiness.
shivpurana:7:39.39	Let fortune go or stay, let death be near, let people revile or praise — the end of sorrow
shivpurana:7:39.4	The radiance of his austerity was such that the gods were amazed; they went again to Shiva and, collected, said:
shivpurana:7:39.40	comes from merit and sin; Shankara always gives happiness. Sometimes Shiva gives sorrow to test,
shivpurana:7:39.41	but in the end he is declared the giver of happiness, being compassionate, without doubt, as gold when refined becomes pure.
shivpurana:7:39.42	So I heard before from the mouth of the sage; so by worshipping him alone I shall gain the highest happiness.
While he was reflecting thus, the boar came within range of release of an arrow.
Shiva too came, close behind the boar; then between the two a wondrous peak was seen.
Its greatness has been told; Shiva went very quickly, Shankara, kind to devotees, to protect Arjuna.
At that moment the two released their arrows: Shiva's arrow at the tail, and Arjuna's at the mouth.
Shiva's arrow entered at the tail, came out quickly through the mouth and disappeared into the ground; [Arjuna's] went out by the tail.
Arjuna's arrow fell at the side; and at that moment the demon boar fell dead on the ground.
The gods felt supreme joy and rained flowers, praising with cries of victory and bowing again and again.
The gods said: "O Lord of all, a single man has undertaken austerity for your sake; whatever that man wants, why do you not give it, O Lord?"
Shiva was pleased at heart and Arjuna came to happiness; the two then looked at the cruel form of the demon.
Arjuna especially, with a happy mind, said: "Ah, this is the best of demons; his form is most wondrous.
He came to kill me; I have been well protected by Shiva; the Lord has given me understanding this very day, without doubt."
Reflecting thus, Arjuna sang "Shiva, Shiva" there, bowed to Shiva again and praised him again and again.
Nandishvara said: Having said this, the gods offered various praises and stood there, their eyes on his feet, their minds steady.
Hearing their words, Shiva, the great Lord of noble mind, laughing and glad at heart, spoke to the gods:
Shiva said: "Go to your own places, all you gods; truly, without doubt, I will accomplish your purpose in every way; there is no doubt."
Nandishvara said: Hearing Shambhu's words, the immortals were fully convinced, and all turned back and went to their own places.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, third book, the Shatarudra Samhita, chapter 40: in the description of the Kirata incarnation, the dialogue of the Bhilla and Arjuna. Nandishvara said: "O all-knowing Sanatkumara, hear the sport of the Supreme Self, full of kindness to devotees and interwoven with the testing of his firmness.
How can an ascetic speak falsely? And know that I am not alone; I serve the leader of a host.
My master is here with many forest Bhillas, able in every way to make war or show favour.
This arrow that you have just taken is his; this arrow will never stay with you.
Why do you wish to lose the fruit of your austerity, ascetic? By theft, deceit, harassment, arrogance and breaking truth
austerity is wasted — this I have heard. So what fruit of austerity will you have today?
So if you do not release the arrow you will be ungrateful; surely my master released the arrow for your sake,
and by it the enemy was killed and the arrow saved again. You are utterly ungrateful, and your austerity brings ill.
You do not speak the truth; how then do you seek success? If you need an arrow, ask my master;
he himself can give many such arrows. My king is here today; why do you seek it like this?
Abandoning gratitude you intend harm; this is not fitting for you; give up this fickleness."
Shiva then quickly sent his own servant for the arrow, and Arjuna too came there.
Nandishvara said: Hearing his words, Partha Arjuna grew angry, remembered Shiva and spoke measured words:
Arjuna said: "Listen, Bhilla, I will speak; your speech is not true. As your birth is, so I know you, forest-dweller.
I am a king and you a thief; how is it fitting to fight? I should fight with the strong, never with the base.
So your master too will be like you. We are declared givers, and you forest-dwellers are thieves.
How should I now ask the king of the Bhillas? Why do you not yourself ask me for an arrow, forest-dweller?
I would give you arrows, for I surely have many; a king would not give up what he has taken.
Why should I give you arrows, forest-dweller? If he wishes anything of me, why does he not come now?
Let your master come; why does he speak through you now? Let him come and, having conquered me in battle,
your master, the leader of the host, take this arrow and go happily to his home. Why the delay?"
Nandishvara said: Hearing these words of Arjuna, whose true strength came from Maheshvara's grace, the Bhilla spoke:
At the same moment the attendant and Arjuna arrived for the arrow; Arjuna rebuked him and took his own arrow.
The Bhilla said: "You are ignorant, not a sage; why do you seek death? Give the arrow and stay happy, or you will meet with trouble."
Nandishvara said: Addressed thus by that Bhilla attendant, shining with Shiva's true power, the Pandava remembered Shankara and said:
Arjuna said: "Hear my words truly, forest-dweller Bhilla: when your master comes, I will show him the fruit.
It is not seemly to fight with you; I will fight with your master. A fight between a lion and a jackal is to be known as laughable.
You have heard my words; today you will see great strength. Go to your master, Bhilla; do as you wish."
Nandishvara said: Addressed thus by Partha, O sage, the Bhilla went to where the Kirata leader of the host, Shiva's incarnation, was.
Then he told in detail all of Arjuna's words to the lord of the Bhillas, the Supreme Self as a Bhilla.
Hearing his words, the lord of the Kiratas was delighted, and Shankara in Bhilla form came with his army.
Then Arjuna the Pandava, seeing the Kirata's army, took his bow with arrows and came to face them.
Then the Kirata sent that messenger again, and through his mouth spoke to the great-souled Bharata:
The attendant said to him there, "Why are you taking the arrow? The arrow is ours; let it go, best of sages."
The Kirata said: "See the army, ascetic; let go the arrow and go now. Why do you seek death now for a small matter?
Your brothers will be stricken with sorrow, and then your wife; the earth will pass from your hands today — that is my view."
Nandishvara said: Thus spoke the Supreme Lord to test Partha's firmness, Shambhu, who had taken form wholly to protect Arjuna.
Addressed thus, that attendant of Shankara came and told the whole matter to Arjuna in detail.
Hearing it, Partha said again to the messenger who had come: "Tell the leader of the host it will turn out the opposite.
If I give you my own arrow, I will be a disgrace to my family, without doubt;
my brothers would surely be stricken with sorrow, and my learning would be fruitless. So let him surely come.
I have never heard of a lion afraid of a jackal; likewise a king is never afraid of a forest-dweller."
Nandishvara said: Addressed thus by the Pandava, he went again to his master and told him all that had been said, in detail.
Then Mahadeva called the Kirata, with his army, hearing that, came with his army to Arjuna.
Addressed thus by the Bhilla's attendant, O best of sages, Arjuna remembered Shankara and said to him:
Arjuna said: "Why do you speak without knowing? You are a fool, forest-dweller. The arrow was released by me today; how can it be yours?
Its shape of lines, its feathers, and it is marked with my name; how has it become yours? Your nature is hard to give up."
Nandishvara said: Hearing his words, that lord of the hosts, the Bhilla, laughed and spoke to Arjuna in the form of a sage:

Listen, ascetic: you are not practising austerity; you are an ascetic by dress only, not truly; you are deceiving.
shivpurana:7:41.0	Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
shivpurana:7:41.0-2	Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.
shivpurana:7:41.1	The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, third book, the Shatarudra Samhita, chapter 41: the description of the incarnation as lord of the Kiratas. Then, seeing him arrive, Arjuna meditated on Shiva, went there and fought a most terrible battle with him.
shivpurana:7:41.10	Meanwhile the god Shiva rose into the sky and fought from there, and Arjuna did likewise.
shivpurana:7:41.11	Leaping up again and again, the god and the prince fought, and the gods were amazed seeing that wondrous battle.
shivpurana:7:41.12	Then Arjuna, knowing it was his turn, remembered Shiva's lotus feet and, gaining true strength from meditating on him, seized him by the feet.
shivpurana:7:41.13	Holding his feet, Arjuna whirled him about; Mahadeva, kind to devotees and maker of wonders, laughed.
shivpurana:7:41.14	To grant him his own service out of subjection to his devotee, O sage, this deed was done by Shiva himself, and could not be otherwise.
shivpurana:7:41.15	Then, laughing right there, Shankara suddenly showed his wondrous, auspicious form out of subjection to his devotee,
shivpurana:7:41.16	as described in the Vedas, scriptures and Puranas, O best of beings, taught by Vyasa for his meditation, which grants all success.
shivpurana:7:41.17	Seeing that beautiful form of Shiva gained through meditation, Arjuna was exceedingly amazed and ashamed.
shivpurana:7:41.18	Ah, this is Shiva himself, whom I chose as my Lord, the Lord of the three worlds himself — alas, what have I now done?
The Lord's maya is powerful, deluding even the masters of maya; what has he done, concealing his form? I have been deceived by the Lord."
With his various hosts and sharp weapons he pressed him hard; pressed by them, Partha remembered his master Shiva.
Reflecting thus in his mind, with folded hands and bowed head, he bowed lovingly to the Lord and, dejected, spoke:
Arjuna said: "God of gods, Mahadeva, compassionate Shankara, Lord of all, my offence should be forgiven by you.
What have you done, concealing your form? I have been deceived by you now. Fie on me, who fought with you, my master, O Lord."
Nandishvara said: Thus the Pandava felt remorse and quickly fell at the feet of Shankara, the great Lord.
Then the Lord, glad at heart, replied to Arjuna, Mahesha, kind to devotees, reassuring him again and again:
Shankara said: "Do not grieve, Partha; you are especially my devotee. I did this today to test you; give up your sorrow."
Nandishvara said: Having said this, the Lord raised Arjuna with his own hands and freed him from shame through his hosts and his own virtues.
Again Shiva spoke to Arjuna, the Pandava esteemed by heroes, delighting him with love in every way, Shankara, kind to devotees:
Shiva said: "O Partha, best of Pandavas, I am pleased; choose a boon. By your blows and strikes today I have accepted worship.
It was done today by my will; there is no offence on your part now. There is nothing I will not give you; choose what you wish.
It has been done well to establish your fame and kingdom over your enemies; do not grieve over this; give up all despondency."
Nandishvara said: Addressed thus by the Lord Shankara, Arjuna, standing attentively, spoke to Shankara with devotion:
Arjuna said: "O good Lord Shambhu, dear to devotees, what is your wish? It should be described by me, O God; you are ever-compassionate Sadashiva."
Having said this, the Pandava then offered to Shankara, the great Lord, a hymn of true devotion consonant with the Veda.
Arjuna said: "Salutations to you, God of gods, salutations to the dweller on Kailasa; Sadashiva, salutations to you, salutations to you, five-faced one.
Salutations to you with matted locks, salutations to you, three-eyed one, to the one of pleasing form, the thousand-faced one.
Nilakantha, salutations to you, salutations to Sadyojata; bull-bannered one, salutations to you, and to the one with Girija on his left side.
Salutations to you, ten-armed one, salutations to you, Supreme Self, to the one with damaru and skull in hand, salutations to you who wear a garland of heads.
To you whose body is like pure crystal and pure camphor, to you with the Pinaka in hand, bearer of the excellent trident,
to you with a tiger skin as upper garment, wearing an elephant hide, to you whose limbs are serpents, salutations; bearer of the Ganga, salutations to you.
Pressed by him, the hosts fled in the ten directions; the lords of the hosts, though urged, did not come back to their master.
Salutations to you with beautiful feet, with reddish feet, served by Nandi and the other hosts, and to you, lord of the Ganas.
Salutations to you in the form of Ganesha, followed by Karttikeya, giver of devotion to devotees and giver of liberation — salutations again and again.
Salutations to you without qualities, salutations again and again to you with qualities, to the formless and the embodied, to the one with parts and without parts.
Salutations to you in the form of a Kirata, who showed me grace, who loves battle with heroes and plays many sports.
Whatever form is seen is remembered as your radiance; you, whose form is consciousness, sport in the three worlds through connection and distinction.
There is no counting your qualities, as there is none of the dust of the earth, of the stars in the sky, or of the drops of rain.
The Vedas cannot count your qualities; how then can I, of dull understanding, O Lord, describe them?
Whatever you are, you are; salutations to you; please show me compassion. I am your servant, O Maheshana; you are my master, O Maheshvara."
Nandishvara said: Hearing his words, Shankara, even more pleased, laughing, spoke again to Arjuna:
Shankara said: "What need of many words? Hear my word: quickly choose a boon, son, and I will give you all of it."
Shiva and Arjuna fought each other with many kinds of weapons, both of great strength and valour.
Nandishvara said: Addressed thus, Arjuna prostrated himself before Sadashiva and, with folded hands and bowed, spoke lovingly in a choked voice:
Arjuna said: "What shall I say, since you abide as the inner controller of all? Still, I have described it today; hear it, O Lord:
the distress from enemies has gone at the sight of you; make it so that I attain success in this world and the highest."
Nandishvara said: Having said this and bowed to Shankara, kind to devotees, Arjuna stood there with shoulders bowed and hands folded.
Shiva too, knowing the Pandava Arjuna to be such, the best of his devotees, was greatly pleased.
Mahesha gave him his own Pashupata weapon, invincible by all at all times, and said these words:
Shiva said: "I have given you my own great weapon; you will be invincible; by it achieve victory over all enemies.
I will tell Krishna, and he will help you; he is my very self, my devotee, the accomplisher of tasks.
By my power, Bharata, rule the kingdom free of thorns, and always have your brother perform various dharmas."
Nandishvara said: Having said this, he placed his own hand on his head, and, quickly worshipped by Arjuna, Shankara vanished.
Shiva too, surely feeling compassion in his mind, approached Arjuna; and Arjuna struck him a firm blow there.
Then Arjuna, glad at heart, having obtained the weapon and the Lord's boon, went to his chief hermitage, remembering Shiva, his teacher, with devotion.
All his brothers were glad, as bodies at the return of life; meeting him they attained happiness, and Draupadi, most virtuous, too.
All the Pandavas, hearing the whole story and that the Supreme Shiva was pleased, could not be sated, and were filled with joy.
In the hermitage a rain of flowers with sandal fell for the good of those great-souled ones.
Bowing joyfully to blessed Shankara, Shiva, they knew the term was over and victory would come.
Meanwhile Krishna, hearing that Arjuna had returned, came to meet him and, hearing the news, was happy:
That is why I told you Shankara removes all sorrow; I serve him always; you too should serve him.
Thus the incarnation of Shankara called Kirata has been told you; hearing it or causing it to be heard, one gains all desires.
Then Shiva cut down all of Arjuna's weapons and all his armour, and only his body remained.
Then Arjuna, remembering Shiva, fought hand to hand with the leader of the host, steadfast though distressed with fear.
With that fight the whole earth with its oceans shook, and the gods fell into distress: "What will happen now?"
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, third book, the Shatarudra Samhita, chapter 42: the description of the twelve Jyotirlinga incarnations. Nandishvara said: "Hear, O sage, of the Lord's twelve supreme incarnations in the form of Jyotirlingas, which work many wonders.
The incarnation of Shankara called Mallikarjuna is the second, on Shrigiri, dear one, granting the fruits devotees desire.
Praised in the form of the linga for the sake of seeing his son, that Shiva went there from his own mountain with great love, O sage.
That second Jyotirlinga, by seeing and worshipping it, O sage, brings great happiness and at the end grants liberation; there is no doubt.
The incarnation of Shankara called Mahakala, dear one, arose in the city of Ujjayini, protector of his own people,
who, when the asura named Dushana, crusher of the dharma of the Vedas, hater of brahmins and destroyer of all, came to Ujjayini,
meditated on by the son of a Vedic brahmin, quickly reduced him, who dwelt in Ratnamala, to ashes with a mere 'hum.'
Having slain him, Mahakala, entreated by the gods, remained in the form of a Jyotirlinga, protector of his devotees.
Seeing and carefully worshipping the linga called Mahakala, one obtains all desires and attains the highest goal.
Omkara, the Supreme Lord, taken on by Shambhu, the Supreme Self, is the fourth incarnation, granting the fruit devotees desire.
Installed with devotion by Vidhi (Vindhya) from his own earthen linga, O sage, Mahadeva appeared, fulfilling the desire of the Vindhya.
Somanatha in Saurashtra, Mallikarjuna on Shrishaila, Mahakala in Ujjayini, and Amareshvara at Omkara,
Entreated by the gods there, he abides in twofold form, granting enjoyment and liberation, in the form of the linga, kind to devotees.
In the pranava was the excellent linga named Omkara, and the earthen one was named Parameshvara, O lord of sages.
Whichever is seen and worshipped is to be known as granting devotees' wishes, O sage — the two most divine Jyotirlingas described to you, great sage.
The fifth incarnation is Kedaresha, the Supreme Shiva, abiding at Kedara in the form of a Jyotirlinga.
Entreated by Nara and Narayana, the incarnations of Hari, O sage, Shiva abides there at Kedara on the snowy mountain,
worshipped by them always, called Kedareshvara; Shambhu grants devotees' wishes by sight and worship.
He is the master of this region, and especially lord of all; that incarnation of Shiva, dear one, grants all desires.
The sixth incarnation of Shambhu, the great Lord, called Bhimashankara, of great sport, is the destroyer of the asura Bhima,
who wondrously protected his devotee named Sudakshina, king of Kamarupa, slaying that asura who tormented devotees.
Named Bhimashankara, he himself abides at Dakini in the form of a Jyotirlinga, Shankara entreated by him.
Kedara on the Himalayan heights, Bhimashankara at Dakini, Vishvesha at Varanasi, Tryambaka on the bank of the Gautami,
The Vishveshvara incarnation arose in Kashi as the seventh, in the form of the whole cosmos, granting enjoyment and liberation, O sage,
always worshipped with devotion by all the gods led by Vishnu, and daily by the lord of Kailasa and by Bhairava too.
He abides there in the form of a Jyotirlinga, granting liberation, the Lord himself of perfected form, in his own city.
Those who with devotion to Kashi and Vishvesha recite their names remain untouched by karma and share in the state of kaivalya.
The eighth, the incarnation called Tryambaka, on the bank of the Gautami, appeared as the moon-crested one, entreated by Gautama.
At Gautama's entreaty he abides there unmoving in the form of a Jyotirlinga, lovingly, wishing to please that sage.
By seeing, touching and worshipping that great Lord, all desires are accomplished, and then there is liberation — ah!
By Shiva's grace the Ganga, named Gautami, abides there out of love for Gautama, purifying and dear to Shankara.
The Vaidyanatha incarnation is declared there the ninth; the Lord of many sports appeared for Ravana's sake.
Making the pretext of being carried by him, Maheshvara was established at Chitabhumi in the form of a Jyotirlinga.
Vaidyanatha at Chitabhumi, Nagesha in Darukavana, Ramesha at the Setubandha, and Ghushmesha at Shivalaya.
He became famous in the three worlds by the name Vaidyanatheshvara; by sight and devoted worship he grants enjoyment and liberation.
The teaching of the greatness of Shiva as Vaidyanatheshvara grants enjoyment and liberation to those who read and hear it, O sage.
The Nageshvara incarnation is declared the tenth; he appeared for his devotee, always punishing the wicked.
Slaying the rakshasa named Daruka, destroyer of dharma, he protected his devotee, the merchant Supriya.
For the benefit of the worlds, bearing the form of a Jyotirlinga, the supreme Shambhu of many sports abides there with Ambika.
Seeing and worshipping that Shiva-linga called Nageshvara, O sage, heaps of great sins are quickly destroyed.
The Rameshvara incarnation is remembered as Shiva's eleventh, bringing joy to Ramachandra and installed by Rama, O sage,
who, well pleased, lovingly gave Rama the boon of victory; Shankara, kind to devotees, appeared as the linga,
and, earnestly entreated by Rama, abides at the Setubandha in the form of a Jyotirlinga, served by Rama, O sage.
The greatness of Rameshvara became wondrous and incomparable on earth, granting enjoyment and liberation and always fulfilling devotees' desires.
These twelve incarnations of Shambhu, the Supreme Self, bring all bliss to men by sight and touch, O sage.
The man who bathes Rameshvara with Ganga water alone, with true devotion, is liberated while living.
Enjoying all pleasures here, even those rare for the gods, and then gaining the highest knowledge, he attains kaivalya, liberation.
The Ghushmeshvara incarnation is the twelfth of Shankara, maker of many sports, giver of joy to Ghushma, kind to devotees.
In the south, O sage, near Devashaila, the Lord appeared in a lake, bringing joy to Ghushma.
Ghushma's son, killed by Sudeha, O sage, Shambhu, pleased by her devotion, kind to devotees, restored whole.
Entreated by her, Shambhu, granting desires, abides in that tank in the form of a Jyotirlinga, called Ghushmeshvara.
Seeing that Shiva-linga and worshipping it with devotion, one enjoys all happiness here and then gains liberation.
Thus the series of Jyotirlingas has been told you by me — twelve, divine, granting enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever reads or hears this story of the Jyotirlingas is freed from all sins and gains enjoyment and liberation.
This Samhita called Shatarudra has been described by me, the good celebration of the hundred incarnations, granting the fruit of all desires.
Of these the first is Somanatha, destroyer of the moon's sorrow; by worship he destroys diseases like consumption and leprosy, O sage.
Whoever reads this daily or hears it with concentration obtains all desires and then surely gains liberation.
The incarnation of Shiva, Somesha, abides in the form of the linga in the auspicious land of Saurashtra, worshipped long ago by the moon.
The Chandrakunda there destroys all sins; bathing there, a wise man is freed from all diseases.
Seeing Someshvara, the great linga, the supreme form of Shiva, one is freed from sin and gains enjoyment and liberation.
[He was] wealthy, supremely generous, a vessel of kindness and virtue, always devoted to Shiva's rites, a Shaiva dear to Shaivas.
Much of his life passed as he practised dharma, but no son was born to him; his wife's seasons were fruitless.
Yet, being intent on knowledge of reality, he did not grieve at this: the self is the self's deliverer and the self's purifier.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, fourth book, the Kotirudra Samhita, chapter 33: the description of the origin and greatness of the Ghushmesha Jyotirlinga. Suta said: Seeing the younger wife's son, the elder was grieved; not bearing her happiness, she quickly turned hostile.
The husband regarded the elder as dear and not the younger, yet that elder then became foul within.
One day the elder, Sudeha, grieving, thought in her heart, "How may my sorrow be quieted?"
Sudeha said: "The fire in my heart will surely be quenched only by the tears of Ghushma's eyes, not otherwise, arising from sorrow.
So today I will kill her sweet-spoken son; whatever is to come after will come — this is my firm resolve."
Suta said: The mean have no discernment of what should and should not be done; the feeling of a co-wife is mostly harsh and self-destroying, O brahmins.
Arjuna then cut down their volleys of arrows; and when they hurled weapons at him in battle, he held fast to Sharva in his mind.
